concept_html:
Coverage tells you which code your tests ran. It does not tell you whether they checked anything. A test whose only assertion is assert result reaches every line and catches almost nothing (lesson B17-L1). Use coverage to find code no test reaches, not as proof of quality.

With pytest-cov 7.1:

pytest --cov=survey_stats --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing --cov-fail-under=90

--cov-branch adds branch coverage. Line coverage counts a line once it runs. Branch coverage also asks whether each if went both ways. A function with if cap is not None: and a single test that passes a cap runs every line, 100% line coverage, but never takes the path where cap is None. The report lists that missed jump as 2->4 in the Missing column, and the file drops to 83%.

--cov-fail-under=90 makes pytest exit with an error when total coverage falls below 90%. Agree a floor with the team and raise it over time. Do not chase 100% with tests that assert nothing.

Markers label tests. Register each one in pyproject.toml, and turn on --strict-markers, so a typo such as @pytest.mark.slwo stops the run instead of creating a new, unused marker:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--strict-markers"
markers = ["slow: takes more than a few seconds"]

Run pytest -m "not slow" while you work, and the full suite in CI. pytest 9 also accepts strict = true, which turns on strict markers along with other strict checks.

A flaky test passes and fails without a code change. Find the cause: a missing seed, shared state, the clock or the network. Never add a retry and move on.

Coverage misses weak assertions. Mutation testing finds them: mutmut 3.8 changes your code in small ways, such as < to <=, and reports every change that no test catches. It automates the habit of breaking the code once.

lines: # markers = ["slow: takes more than a few seconds"]
@pytest.mark.parametrize(
("weight", "cap", "expected"),
[(5, 3, 3), (2, 3, 2), (5, None, 5)],
def test_capped(weight, cap, expected):
assert capped(weight, cap=cap) == expected

exercises.prompt_html:
risk_band(score) is already imported in your test file:

def risk_band(score: float | None) -> str:
    if score is None:
        return "unknown"
    if score >= 0.8:
        return "high"
    if score >= 0.5:
        return "medium"
    return "low"

Write tests, as functions whose names start with test_, that run every branch and catch an off-by-one change. The checker measures which lines your tests run, then runs them against two changed versions: >= 0.8 becomes > 0.8, and >= 0.5 becomes > 0.5. Your tests must fail for both.
solution_lines: @pytest.mark.parametrize(
pytest.param(None, "unknown", id="missing"),
pytest.param(0.8, "high", id="at-0.8"),
pytest.param(0.79, "medium", id="below-0.8"),
pytest.param(0.5, "medium", id="at-0.5"),
pytest.param(0.49, "low", id="below-0.5"),
def test_risk_band(score: float | None, expected: str) -> None:
assert risk_band(score) == expected

title: Coverage, markers and a test suite you can trust in CI
why_html: A pricing module had 96% line coverage, and the team was proud of it. Branch coverage was 71%. Every else path that handled a missing discount code was untested, including one that applied a 100% discount. It shipped and cost a client three days of free orders. --cov-branch with a 90% floor would have blocked the merge and pointed at the exact branches.
